reaction_type: Hypersensitivity reaction (HSR): fever, rash, GI symptoms, respiratory symptoms
risk_if_positive: ~50% risk of clinically suspected HSR; ~100% positive predictive value for immunologically confirmed HSR in carriers
recommendation: Do not prescribe abacavir. Use alternative NRTI (tenofovir alafenamide or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate). HLA-B*57:01 testing is mandatory before first abacavir prescription.
alternative_drugs: tenofovir alafenamide, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, zidovudine
text_chunk: HLA-B*57:01 and abacavir hypersensitivity: The PREDICT-1 randomized trial (Mallal et al., NEJM 2008) demonstrated that prospective HLA-B*57:01 screening before abacavir initiation eliminated immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity reactions (0% vs 2.7% in control arm). Negative predictive value approaches 100%. HSR typically occurs within first 6 weeks, presenting with multi-organ involvement. Rechallenge after HSR can be fatal due to rapid-onset cardiovascular collapse. This is the most widely implemented PGx test globally and is considered the exemplar of successful pharmacogenomic implementation.

reaction_type: Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
risk_if_positive: Odds ratio >80 for SJS/TEN; absolute risk 5-25% depending on dose and renal function
recommendation: Do not prescribe allopurinol. Use alternative urate-lowering therapy (febuxostat, probenecid). Pre-prescription screening is recommended in high-prevalence populations.
text_chunk: HLA-B*58:01 and allopurinol-induced SCAR: Allopurinol is the most common cause of SJS/TEN in many countries. The association with HLA-B*58:01 was first identified in Han Chinese (Hung et al., PNAS 2005) with OR ~580. The allele is most prevalent in Korean (12%), Southeast Asian (6-8%), and African American (3-4%) populations. Taiwan implemented nationwide screening in 2010, reducing allopurinol-associated SJS/TEN incidence by >90%. Renal impairment and higher allopurinol doses increase risk in carriers. Mortality from SJS/TEN is 10-30%; survivors often have long-term sequelae.

risk_if_positive: Odds ratio >100 for SJS/TEN in Southeast Asian populations; relative risk varies by ethnicity
recommendation: Do not prescribe carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine. Use alternative anticonvulsant (levetiracetam, valproate, lamotrigine, lacosamide). FDA mandates testing in patients with Asian ancestry.
text_chunk: HLA-B*15:02 and carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN: First reported by Chung et al. (Nature 2004) in Han Chinese with OR >2500. The association is predominantly observed in Southeast Asian populations where HLA-B*15:02 prevalence is 4-12%. SJS/TEN involves widespread epidermal necrosis mediated by granulysin-expressing cytotoxic T cells. FDA issued a safety alert in 2007 requiring HLA-B*15:02 testing before carbamazepine use in patients of Asian ancestry. The risk extends to oxcarbazepine and possibly phenytoin.

reaction_type: Maculopapular exanthema (MPE), DRESS, SJS/TEN (all types of carbamazepine hypersensitivity)
risk_if_positive: Odds ratio 8-25 for any carbamazepine hypersensitivity reaction across all ethnicities
recommendation: Consider alternative anticonvulsant. If carbamazepine is necessary, start at low dose with close monitoring. Risk applies across all ethnic groups unlike HLA-B*15:02.
text_chunk: HLA-A*31:01 and carbamazepine hypersensitivity: Unlike HLA-B*15:02, which is specific to SJS/TEN, HLA-A*31:01 is associated with the full spectrum of carbamazepine hypersensitivity reactions across all ethnic groups including Europeans. McCormack et al. (NEJM 2011) demonstrated the association in Europeans and Japanese. CPIC recommends considering HLA-A*31:01 testing before carbamazepine initiation, particularly in European populations where HLA-B*15:02 is rare but HLA-A*31:01 prevalence is ~5%.

risk_if_positive: Odds ratio 3-18 for SJS/TEN in Southeast Asian populations (weaker than carbamazepine association)
recommendation: Consider alternative anticonvulsant in HLA-B*15:02 positive patients. If phenytoin is necessary, use with caution and close dermatologic monitoring.
text_chunk: HLA-B*15:02 and phenytoin-induced SJS/TEN: The association is weaker than with carbamazepine but clinically significant. Locharernkul et al. (Epilepsia 2008) reported OR 18.5 in Thai patients. CPIC recommends that HLA-B*15:02 positive patients should avoid phenytoin and other aromatic anticonvulsants. Phenytoin-induced SJS/TEN may also be influenced by CYP2C9 poor metabolizer status (elevated drug levels).

risk_if_positive: Odds ratio 3-27 for SJS/TEN in Southeast Asian populations; cross-reactivity with carbamazepine-associated risk
recommendation: Avoid oxcarbazepine in HLA-B*15:02 positive patients. Use alternative anticonvulsant. Cross-reactivity with carbamazepine risk is expected due to structural similarity.
text_chunk: HLA-B*15:02 and oxcarbazepine-induced SJS/TEN: Oxcarbazepine is structurally related to carbamazepine, and cross-reactivity for HLA-B*15:02-mediated SJS/TEN is documented. Chen et al. (Neurology 2017) reported increased risk in HLA-B*15:02 carriers. FDA labeling for oxcarbazepine includes a warning about HLA-B*15:02 and recommends testing in patients of Asian ancestry.

reaction_type: Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS): fever, rash, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy
risk_if_positive: Odds ratio 7-20 for DHS; ~1-2% absolute risk in carriers in endemic areas
recommendation: Consider HLA-B*13:01 testing before dapsone initiation in at-risk populations. Use alternative agents (clofazimine, minocycline) for leprosy if positive.
text_chunk: HLA-B*13:01 and dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome: Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome occurs in 0.5-3% of patients receiving dapsone for leprosy or dermatitis herpetiformis. Zhang et al. (NEJM 2013) identified HLA-B*13:01 as a strong predictor in Chinese patients (OR 20.5). The association has been replicated in other Asian populations. Pre-treatment screening is particularly relevant in leprosy-endemic regions where dapsone is a WHO-recommended therapy.

risk_if_positive: Elevated risk of SJS/TEN, particularly in Japanese and Korean populations where *15:11 is more common than *15:02
recommendation: Avoid carbamazepine. Use alternative anticonvulsant. HLA-B*15:11 is in the HLA-B75 serotype along with *15:02 and shares epitopes relevant to carbamazepine presentation.
text_chunk: HLA-B*15:11 and carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN: HLA-B*15:11 belongs to the same HLA-B75 serological group as HLA-B*15:02 and shares critical residues in the antigen-binding groove. Kaniwa et al. (Pharmacogenomics 2008) reported the association in Japanese patients where *15:11 is more prevalent than *15:02. Extended HLA-B75 serotype testing may capture additional at-risk individuals beyond *15:02 alone.

risk_if_positive: Odds ratio ~13 for ticlopidine-induced liver injury
recommendation: Consider alternative antiplatelet agent (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor). HLA-A*33:03 testing may be considered before ticlopidine initiation.
text_chunk: HLA-A*33:03 and ticlopidine-induced hepatotoxicity: Ticlopidine causes cholestatic liver injury in ~1% of users. Hirata et al. (Pharmacogenomics J 2008) identified HLA-A*33:03 as a risk factor in Japanese patients. Ticlopidine use has declined with the availability of clopidogrel and newer P2Y12 inhibitors, but the association illustrates HLA-mediated drug-induced liver injury.

risk_if_positive: Odds ratio ~8 for lapatinib-induced liver injury; ~2% incidence in carriers
recommendation: Monitor liver function tests closely if lapatinib is prescribed. Consider alternative HER2-targeted therapy (trastuzumab, pertuzumab, neratinib) if available.
text_chunk: HLA-DRB1*07:01 and lapatinib-induced liver injury: Spraggs et al. (JAMA 2011) identified HLA-DRB1*07:01 as a risk factor for lapatinib hepatotoxicity in breast cancer patients. Unlike most HLA-drug associations (MHC class I), this involves an MHC class II allele, suggesting a CD4+ T cell-mediated mechanism. The high prevalence of the risk allele (~25% in Europeans) but low absolute risk (~2% DILI incidence) limits its clinical utility for screening.

risk_if_positive: Odds ratio ~80 for flucloxacillin-induced liver injury; but low absolute risk (~1 in 500-1000 carriers)
recommendation: Be aware of elevated DILI risk. Monitor liver function during flucloxacillin therapy. Consider alternative antistaphylococcal antibiotic if alternative available.
text_chunk: HLA-B*57:01 and flucloxacillin-induced liver injury: Daly et al. (Nature Genetics 2009) identified the GWAS association between HLA-B*57:01 and flucloxacillin DILI (OR ~80). This is the same HLA allele associated with abacavir HSR but causes a different type of adverse reaction (hepatotoxicity vs systemic HSR). The high OR but low absolute risk (~1 in 500-1000 exposed carriers) makes routine screening less cost-effective than for abacavir.

risk_if_positive: Elevated risk of SCAR, though lower than with allopurinol; limited case reports suggest association
recommendation: Exercise caution when prescribing febuxostat to HLA-B*58:01 positive patients, particularly those with prior allopurinol SCAR. Consider probenecid as alternative.
text_chunk: HLA-B*58:01 and febuxostat-induced SCAR: While febuxostat is generally recommended as an alternative to allopurinol in HLA-B*58:01 positive patients, rare case reports have documented SJS/TEN and DRESS with febuxostat in HLA-B*58:01 carriers. The shared xanthine oxidase inhibitor mechanism may present cross-reactivity risk. The evidence is limited compared to the robust allopurinol-HLA-B*58:01 association, but caution is warranted.
